Mato, perhaps he descended from Borak. Who knows? Martin, Blasko's son, I think that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question, that some of these young men you were at Borak, it's quite possible that they when Borak fell they came back through the village.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were fleeing, they passed through the village, that's possible. They had been at the line and then withdrew and passed through the village. She withdrew with the elderly, because there was Blaz, Martin's brother and Sofija they're still alive. But Martin and Kata didn't pull through.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And just in terms of how Blaz came to escape, it's the fact that the young soldiers came back from the front line and effectively collected Blaz and took him away to safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't collect them. He fled down to the fields below where Stojanovic was working. Panic spread. Civilians had fled. There were some other people who were saved. Mato must have returned and told them. Martin and Kata, perhaps, thought that they could escape by going to the basement. They thought they could perhaps hide themselves there, but they didn't survey of. Whereas Blasko and that brother and Sofija, they also lived there in Kriz, that's Martin's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Look, I understand. It's very helpful for you to provide that detail too, and if I could ask you this: At least as far as Kriz is concerned, it appears from what you saw and what you were told that the soldiers from Borak, the HVO soldiers from Borak, pulled back and went through the village of Kriz in retreat, and on their way through the civilians, many of the civilians panicked and started to run as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some went to the village if they had their parents there. Some soldiers fled down by the stream. They didn't pass through the village. But if some of them had family members in the village, they perhaps went to the village. But you couldn't even see them. They were fleeing, shouting out. You wouldn't have time to speak to them, to ask them whether their relatives were alive. And then two or three days later you might see them in Prozor in a drunken state, and they would tell you various stories. But some survived, others didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, there's something I want to put to your from the book as well now and ask for your comment again. Would you mind going, please, to page 34 and 35, the entry on Kata Ratkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kata Ratkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's correct. The part I'm interested in -- I won't get you to read the whole thing out, but the part I'm interested in is in the last couple of sentences after describing the army's -- Muslim soldiers of the BH army killed her in the brother's basement, did the -- does the text say that their son who tries to -- tries to save and defend them is shot by the soldiers, but they can't catch him. Effectively, he gets away.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the son Fabjan. There is no other son. But I don't know whether he was wounded, whether it was in Borak or the village or below the village. I don't know. But he still lives in the village now, and he has something in his head, and the doctors can't take this out. He has some shrapnel in his head and the doctors can't extract the shrapnel. Someone must have thrown a grenade or done something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, are you aware of whether -- sorry, I'll just stick to the first couple of facts first. Is it within your knowledge that -- that Fabjan did in fact come along and fight with the Bosnian army soldiers near to his mother and father's house?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know where he fought, whether it was in Borak or when withdrawing from Kriz. And I don't know which direction they were fleeing in or where they went. And I don't know where Fabjan fled. Perhaps it was along the stream too. Perhaps he didn't even pass through the area where his parents lived, whereas Mato went to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And just -- just -- Mato's family name, I'm sorry, just -- would you confirm that again, please?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mato Ratkic. Ratkic. He fled. He told the others to flee. They fled to Blaz's cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Are you able to say whether at the time when Mato gave the instruction or suggestion to flee whether or not there were already buildings on fire in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the upper village in Kriz. The stables at the top of the hill, they were all on fire. There weren't many houses that had burnt down below, only Mato's house, but up on the top of the hill there were stables and they'd all burnt down. And the first houses, the houses immediately in the vicinity of Borak, Serafina's and Franc Stojanovic's houses, these houses were also affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: At the time when this flight from Kriz took place, I understand -- sorry, I'll ask the question a different way. I understand that by the time you arrived it was full daylight. Did the people tell you what the lighting conditions were like when they fled from Kriz, when these incidents happened at Kriz? Had day dawned yet or was it still dark?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 6.00. They said in Kriz it was about 5.00. I don't know. The people who were in Cer said 6.00. In Kriz they said 5.00 or half past 5.00, but it was at daybreak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So is it fair to describe the lighting conditions as not pitch black but still fairly dim, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether the visibility was good at the time because some were sleeping. I'm surprised that my folk didn't let the livestock out. My mother was sleeping. The livestock were set on fire. But some people released the livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you for those answers. I'll press on now. Now, you indicated that Franc and Serafina Stojanovic were seen, but they were in a position where you were not able to go and inspect what happened to them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were stripped down to their underwear. I don't know who did that. But there's Ruza Stojanovic and Cvita Stojanovic who were also there. Their houses were in that area. Cvita and Ruza managed to save themselves. They still live there. One of them lives where Franjo's house is, and Ruza lives on the other side of the stream. They are alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did you know how they got away?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cvita was captured near Zadruga in the direction of Rajici on the road. They were where the old shop was. We used to call it the old shop. That's where they were captured with Sofija Stojanovic and those children, Jela Dzalto's children. A young man from Here captured them there and released them later. They were saved. I don't know whether we gave some money or not, but they were saved. They are both alive and the three children are alive, and there's Sofija and her sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Could we move on now to the Prskalo house. Now, we're moving really to the Rajici area, so perhaps if the witness could be shown the third of those, which I think will be P305. Very well. Now, the Prskalo house was the house owned by the commander of the 3rd Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father owned the house, and he was his father's son. He was the commander at the school building, and there was his command there, some people. But that was not where he slept. He slept in the school. And there were some civilians from Bobari, too. Sofija and Jela and the kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And did some of those get away and escape?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sofija now lives in Austria. She managed to save their three children and their aunt. All the children and Stenko are now in Austria, and Mijo, too, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Prskalo, the commander of the battalion, leave any weapons there in the house so that they could defend themselves if an attack came along, even when he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I never entered his house. I really can't say. Not before the war and not during. I hadn't been in that house for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now you recall Jela Dzalto. I'm sorry about the pronunciation of that name, but Jela Dzalto.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She was in Bobari. Marko was there too and Zora, all of them from Bobari. They got down to Uzdol and then to Rajici because they were near the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Now, as far as Jela goes, could I ask you to look, please, at page 66 -- or could I just before -- I'll take you to the book. I just want to ask you a general question first. Are you aware of whether or not Jela Dzalto went into the house and returned the fire of the Bosnian army soldiers from the house?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Her sister told me that she used foul language. She had forgotten something apparently. Her children and her sister came as far as the cooperative, and they were captured there. They left them behind in the shop and told not to move. They were saved eventually, but she went back to the house and the house burned down, and she burned down inside the house. I can't tell you whether she'd been wounded previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are you aware of any eyewitnesses to her death?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Sofija. I know about her children. And that's what Sofija says, that she remained there. Her brother-in-law Josip Dzalto, nicknamed Bikan, took the road to Donja Vas. He took his wife and daughter along. He just sped past them and left them where they were. One of them was killed, and the remaining three were saved and are now in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Could I just -- I was going to come to Josip Dzalto in a minute, but since you've raised him, I'll ask you now. Where was Josip Dzalto living on the morning when these troubles happened?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josip Dzalto was living with his -- what's his name? His relative Emil Piplica. It's near Budim, Mendesi, thereabouts. Budim is up on the hill and Mendesi is further down the road. Jozo Kodzani [phoen], Emil Piplica, Zora Mendes, Josip Mendes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did Josip take his family and leave the village when these -- when these Bosnian army soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And was he --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had fled before this time because in Donja Vas he had a son-in-law and his daughter was married to this man so he drove through Donja Vas and on to Prozor and he left the others behind. I'm not sure why he decided to do that. He just -- he drove this bus, and he just sped past them. He didn't have time to stop and -- and wait for them to board, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just stopping there for a moment. My next question was, just to be clear: On -- did he leave the village -- whatever he'd done in the past, did he leave the village on the morning of this tragedy, that's being the 14th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that morning. I'm not sure about the time. It may have been 2.00 or 3.00. He just escaped. He left Uzdol. He went to his daughter's and her husband's place in Donja Vas. The distance is perhaps two or three kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the way as he drove out of his -- out of the village of Uzdol, did he pass by some of the other people who were also fleeing from the village?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who was it that he passed by?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was when he fled. All I'm saying is Sofija, Jelena's sister, were there, and he left them behind. I'm not sure what time he drove by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand you can't give a precise time but I'm just trying to get a general approximate time. What time was it or what -- at approximately what point was it when he passed Sofija by? Was it before she'd been taken captive and put in the shop or was it after that?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before. Before she was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. So that whatever time it was, this Josip drove past her while she was fleeing from her house but before she was captured by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this road. He had to drive by Jaka's field and house. His wife was staying over at Prskalo's house, and he was with his relative. Sofija knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did he collect anyone from the Prskalo house?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one. No one. He just collected his wife. I'm not sure if he brought his children, and he drove straight to his son-in-law's place where his daughter was, too, and he drove them to Prozor too. But not through Uzdol. There's another road through Donja Vas and Kransko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I've got some questions about this Prskalo. Was he an HVO soldier? Sorry, I take that back. That question was wrong. The questions were about this Josip, not Prskalo. Josip, the man who was driving.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an HVO driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was he on duty that morning or not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would bring supplies in. He was off duty that night. There were several drivers working for the HVO and he happened to be off duty on that particular night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was he in uniform that particular night when he was driving the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to be. All soldiers were in uniform. No one was allowed to move about in civilian clothes. People didn't know each other. There were soldiers there from Rama, from Orasti [phoen], from Ceko [phoen]. As soon as they saw someone moving around in civilian clothes, it might have occurred to them this person was a deserter. Everyone had to be in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Was he armed on that morning?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't see him on that day. I later heard from his - what's her name? - wife's sister. We shouted, Stop, and he said, I'll come back to fetch you, and he took the roundabout route because they were shooting over there, so he took the other road, not the one along the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle was he driving?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some sort of a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I want to turn to the -- the other four people that were killed in that area. This was Sima and Mara, and also nearby Stanko and Lucija Rajic. With respect to these people, three of them were killed right next to each other and Mara was killed quite nearby; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nearby, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And Mara was an HVO member, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mara helped us out at the beginning. She was a bit older, still single.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: She was a -- she had a fighting spirit, though, didn't she, Mara?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what she had. I know she sang very nicely. She sang with the choir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me just ask you to look at page 52 of the book, please. That's the entry for Mara Rajic. I want to take you to the passage where it describes -- commencing at the beginning of the war, that part. I don't need to know all the background details. But does it say here: "At the beginning of the war she volunteers, become a member of the HVO and works in the kitchen as chef. She is brave and proud of her religion and nationality, often encouraging the younger kitchen girls and even the soldiers themselves. She says to them, If you don't have enough soldiers, get me a rifle and I'll take the next shift." Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, is that information accurate that I've just read out from the book?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mara was, was Mara, quite brave, but there were soldiers there. She would be telling them what to eat and what not to eat. Some didn't want to eat the beans and some didn't want to eat the soup, and some didn't want to eat something else. They were difficult to handle. But Mara wasn't there all the time. She was just there at the beginning, but she was part of the war in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because she was supposed to receive the same thing as the other one, because there were other women and each had to bake two or three loaves of bread. They should get some sort of a certificate by way of gratitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I just want to ask you some questions about the houses from which these persons that we've just talked about tried to escape and started to run. In respect to Sima and Mara, were there any HVO soldiers who were living in that house at the time who got away?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in their house. Only Mara was there with her mother. That's across the way from Prskalo's house. She -- he died before the war. He was a handyman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. At the Prskalo's house were there any HVO soldiers living there or staying there at the time of these killings?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The one over there, Dzalto, and then Mara and Sima probably went. There was a newer, better house over there, more modern. And Stanko. Stanko's house was the first or -- the fourth one behind Jaka's house. First Jaka's house, Ivana's house, and then Mija's house, and then old Domin's house, and then Stanko's house is the last. Stanko and Lucija came from that house. If they hadn't made it to the other house, God knows what would have happened to them if they spent the night there or if they'd gone to Prskalo's house. I have no idea what would have happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. When you passed by those houses did you notice whether the walls had been hit with machine-gun fire or bullet fire or indeed suffered any marks of war, and I mean the external walls of the house? I'm speaking of the houses in the Rajici area at the moment.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't look. I only looked at the people. Prskalo's house was on fire. Now, whether it was or not, I don't know. There was a lot of smoke all around the house. The lower end of the road no houses were set on fire. Only Stanko's cowshed was on fire, right next to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I understand those. Thank you for answering those questions, and I understand it takes an effort to answer them. I want to turn now to some issues about what happened afterwards. Now, I want to ask you first of all were there any prisoners taken from the Bosnian army by the HVO forces to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When, do you mean? Yes, later. They got one of them. That was later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, I don't mean later. I mean on the morning.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean alive? No, no one was taken alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several soldiers of the BH army. They were given a burial behind the school building in spot, and I think they've been moved to Scipe since, but I can't say how many exactly. I think five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three people came. They exhumed the bodies and moved the bodies to Scipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thank you. I understand. I just wanted to know whether you were aware of any prisoners being taken. You say no. That's fine. We'll move on. Now, as to the surviving --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some dead bodies there. I don't know about the count. I didn't look carefully. And some people came and took them to Scipe. Not immediately. Some time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, were there -- were there 12 HVO soldiers who lost their lives on that morning?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Were some of those soldiers the crew of the tank that was positioned at the school?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, three, I think. They had positions at Prozor, so I saw some people I didn't know, and they came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were some of the other -- of the other 12 HVO soldiers killed young men who were killed during the fight in the school building and around it?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was there that what's his name was killed, Josip Maric, at the school building, and the others were all other the place. Behind the school building, outside the school building, all over Cer, because what the hamlet is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Apart from Ivo were any of the HVO soldiers that were killed, killed in or near to the hamlets Kriz, Rajici, and Zelenike?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not there. Pero Kovcalija in Cer and Slavko Mendes over there. Just down from Ivo's house. So it's all Cer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, as to Slavko Mendes, how close to his body did you see the bodies of any Bosnian soldiers, any ABiH soldiers? I shouldn't have said Bosnian. I'm sorry about that. Let me ask the question again. How near to Slavko Mendes's body did you notice the bodies of any soldiers from the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a road there forking off into four different roads. He was just off the road and the other one was maybe 15 metres into the houses up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- all right. I've got some questions about what happened to the survivors. I don't need to know each individual one. But was there an organised way in which the survivors were taken to Prozor or did they all make their own way there in various different ways?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All in their own different ways. The -- all of them walked or ran. No one had any means of transportation as far as I know. No vehicles were available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware of whether they were all gathered together at any point whilst in Prozor? I mean the survivors.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Uzdol the whole day. Where they brought them, I don't know. There were plenty of our people in Prozor. I had many relatives there, but apart from that I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Were you involved in the taking of statements about what happened from any of those survivors?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone sees me and someone sees another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The video that was shown to your in part by the Prosecution yesterday, do you recall who was the person holding the camera when that video was taken?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his name was. He wasn't one of ours. I think he was from Rama.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from that video -- what time of day was that video taken?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Some followed us with a small camera and some were recording, and maybe some other people were recording footage too. I don't know. Everything was being videoed. I don't know. Until dusk. Two cameras came, one small and one large. I don't know who recorded what. There was this guy who had a larger camera, but he only came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did the BBC come the following day? I mean, international news coverage? Did a crew from there come --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I don't know because I only came the next day. I'd been in Prozor with the chief, the president, whatever. We had to be on our way to Split doing something or other over there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall when it was that the bodies of the HVO soldiers, I mean the military people, the young men who were killed, do you recall when it was that their bodies were removed from the Uzdol village? Was it the same day or was it later?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think later. First the civilians went to Split because they buried the soldiers in Prozor immediately, and the others were waiting over there for a week or even longer. It was a long wait. It was difficult to cope. You knew they were dead, and you didn't know whether they would bury them or not. It was a very difficult wait, even if they were already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the decision to leave the civilian deceased where they were for more than a day?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire day. Some were dragged further down, and those from Kriz could not be brought over, and some were buried the same day. There weren't enough vehicles to go around, so they went to all the different places, and eventually there was a lorry that took them to Prozor. I don't know who brought that. Someone had ordered for them to be taken to Split, the chief over there, the municipality president, Misko Jozic. What do I know. The command. What's his name? The Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, you had no involvement in yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I had to provide information on their -- the years of birth. Some people from Bugojno, the tank crew operators. We had no idea about them. I don't know. I gave them whatever I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, were you -- did you see a British journalist named Kate Adie and her support crew escorted into the village of Uzdol by HVO officers at any time?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Someone came. I'm not sure about their names. Beats me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you see any representative of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees arrive in the village?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? The same day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... follow.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I spent more time in Prozor. It was all the same to me. All of my relatives had been killed. My sister had come over from Usiga [phoen]. I was sort of half conscious for the following days. I had no idea where I was. I may have gone to Uzdol as well, but I can't remember now. Until the burial took place; it's all hazy to me. There was some people attending the funeral, some relatives from Dubrovnik and Split. I didn't even realise they were there attending a funeral. They took pictures at the funeral. I simply failed to realise at the time that they were around at all. I had no idea. It was all so hazy to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I think you've maybe cut off a list of questions that I was going to ask you. Could I ask you a general question. Your memory of the incidents of the following days is fairly incomplete because you were in a very upset state. Is that a accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was devoid of will. I was -- my wife came over. She was half falling down. I was sort of half conscious myself, and I had to take care of my wife and family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think in light of that, I'm not going to ask you some questions that I had in mind for that period. And the last thing I want to ask you about now - and this is the last questions in the cross-examination altogether - concerns some combat reports that -- HVO combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And I just ask that the witness please be shown the first of these. There's a bundle of them, and this is -- sorry, excuse me. This is Defence 65 ter number 238. It is uploaded on this occasion, DD001200. And it's to be MFI 318, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What's coming up on the screen now you may or may not have seen these documents and I'll ask you that, but what they appear to be is battle reports or combat reports concerning what happened at Uzdol, and I'll just ask you some questions about it. If you can answer, do. If you can't, tell us.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have in front of you now a document that appears to be on the face of it a combat report dated 14th of September under the hand of Colonel Zeljko Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 0700 hours? Do you see that? Okay. Could I just ask you this first of all: You were familiar with Colonel Siljeg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard of him, but I did not know him personally. I never had direct contact with him, but I had heard about Siljeg and someone called Praljak. I don't think he was in our area, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person who gave you the order to get from Prozor quickly back to Uzdol to help out? Who gave you the order to get moving?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the morning? No one issued the order, but when I heard at that Uzdol was burning, I went there. And the others who were there in Prozor that evening, we went there on our own. Ivica Rajic said there's a relative of mine. He entered Prozor or was halfway there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. I just want to ask you whether or not you're able to comment on this. First of all, did you ever see this order before today -- or this combat report before today?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it before. I've heard of this person, but I do not know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. As far as the information in it, though, is it accurate that -- that there was, in fact, fierce fighting in Uzdol or that the MOS -- could you just explain to the Tribunal what's the MOS?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MOS, the Muslim armed forces, later the ABiH. You have the HVO, the Croatian forces. Then there were the Serbian forces. And MOS, I suppose that was the Muslim armed forces initially, which later became the ABiH, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever hear of a man called Stjepan Siber, a Croat who was a member of the -- a deputy commander of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stjepan Siber. I haven't heard of him. I've heard with -- what was his name? Divjak, Jovan Divjak, but I haven't heard of the other name you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Did you hear of Stjepan Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He was a person of Croatian ethnicity involved in the Bosnian government from the very start, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was in Sarajevo. I don't know what he did there. I've seen him on television. He smoked a pipe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I did distract on the MOS question. That was really my fault. Let me just persist here. To your knowledge, as this combat order reflects, there was in fact heavy fighting in Uzdol between the time 6.00 in the morning and 7.00 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I arrived there later. When I arrived there, the soldiers were no longer there. The ABiH troops had withdrawn to Here. I

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I arrived there later. When I arrived there, the soldiers were no longer there. The ABiH troops had withdrawn to Her. I didn't see a single soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, I think rather than putting these orders -- this order you, I'll just ask you some general questions about what you heard in particular about these matters. First of all, you were told that before your arrival the HVO had been the subject of a strong attack by the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that they would attack Crni Vrh. There was some sort of line-up there. Our line was further away in the direction of Prozor and Vakuf. They were expecting an attack up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But -- but after you left Prozor and came to Uzdol, you were told there had been a fierce, strong attack made by the Bosnian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a fierce attack that they carried out. As to the extent to which our people defended themselves around the school and in Cer, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But you also heard by the time you got there that the attack had been repulsed and that the -- that the attack, as far as you could see, was not continuing on the area of the school in Cer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had all fled around the school and the vicinity. I don't know whether they -- there were people who had been killed or whether they had withdrawn themselves. Our people said that they had repulsed the attack but perhaps the soldiers had returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as well as those pieces of information, you heard that -- from your soldiers that the HVO had used some very heavy artillery shelling in order to get rid of the Bosnian soldiers from the hamlets. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. They had opened fire, but I don't know what sort of equipment they had. I heard the shooting, the shelling, but the fighting wasn't really in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand that. But those artillery weapons that the HVO had, those artillery weapons were not sighted on or aimed at your hamlets, your Uzdol hamlets. They were sighted on and aimed at ABiH positions and also the village of Here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably. Our men wouldn't fire on their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course not. And so therefore when there was fighting -- well, I won't use the word "fighting." Perhaps I'll put it another way. When there was the presence of Bosnian soldiers -- Bosniak soldiers, Bosnian soldiers, in the hamlets, the artillery weapons had to find their range when they were shooting at those targets. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. That's something for the command to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I think the witness has answered. The witness has been consistently asked about things he really does not know about. I have held my council up to now, but now it's come to a point, he has been asked about the war, the tactics, and the witness has been very clear he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Morrissey, I believe that maybe those questions should be addressed to some other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm in a difficult position because I was going to disagree with the objection but the answer that he gave already has really squashed me and that is that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So that puts an end to the controversy, Your Honour. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Listen, I'm just going to -- as a matter of thoroughness, I'm going to ask you to look at the documents which were on the screen a minute ago. Those are the combat orders, there's three of them, and this is the last of the series of questions and then I've finished. That first order that you looked at, the one with the time at 7.00, you agree that as far as the facts are set out in that order, you have no dispute with what's said in that order from your own knowledge. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who wrote this report. Commanders did. I have not got the right to comment on it. I'll maintain a neutral position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you to pick a fight with superiors past or present, just to confirm what your experience was. Would you look at the second one of those orders. There's one over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The witness might need have to have the page turned over for him now. There's another report at 8.00 in the morning, 0800 hours. And can we just turn over the page to that, please. It's DD001205 in English, and it will be another page number in B/C/S or -- it's page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you have that on the screen in front you, an interim report, situation at 0800 hours? I'll just make sure everyone's got that on the screen before I start asking questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We don't have that on the screen, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me a moment, please, Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm told it's the second page in English as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this document here you indicate you've never seen the document. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these people, Rado Nikolic, Draga Batinic, Niku Kolak, Himzo Sehic. I don't know these people of theirs. I have never heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In any event, I'm not going to query you about them because it's not particular they are talking an Uzdol in that particular section. Maybe they are; maybe they're not. But it's the about the bottom part that I'm interested in here. It says: "Having fighting is under way in Uzdol. We are opening fire from all artillery and tank pieces. We are sending reinforcements. The MOS are at 50 metres from the school. They are encircling the hamlets of Kriz and Zelenike." Now, what did you understand to be the position at 8.00 a.m.? Was that the position, the one that is reported in this order here?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They were using their artillery to shell. Heavy artillery was being used to shell those positions. But they didn't help at all because these people were all killed. It says 6.00 to 7.00, but here it says up to 8.00. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm just not sure which you're looking at when you say it says 6.00 to 7.00. You may not be looking at the same page.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see a report with the situation. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Interim report, an interim report with the situation at 0800 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same I'm looking at too. Okay. Well, you see that it says there that: We're opening fire from artillery and tank poises. Sending in reinforcements, and the MOS are 50 metres from the school. What I'm asking you is: Were you there at 8.00 and can you confirm that that's the fact or can you not comment?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "shelled," but I don't know where, because the people who died, the Bosniak, et cetera, they didn't -- they weren't killed in Uzdol. I don't know where else there was fighting. It says Citluk up here. These people weren't in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll turn over to the page to the next one, please, and this is a situation report, interim report, situation at 1000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This will be page 4 in English. It's the third page in Bosnian and the fourth in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have that on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll ask you the question as always first of all: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. As to the material --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has to do with Doljani, Kucani. Our lines weren't there. I haven't seen any of these documents. I haven't seen the first one, the second one, or the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm not exactly concerned about the Kucani, Slatina and Doljani sector. What I'm concerned about was the report at the top of the first paragraph where it says: "In the Uzdol sector fighting is still under way. The MOS stormed into parts of Kriz and Zelenike hamlets. Uzdol was under a threat of becoming completely surrounded. After the introduction of fresh troops the MOS attack subsided in strength." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It says up to 1000 hours, and I know there were people who had been killed in the house, and I saw other people who had been killed at the time. There was no fighting. I had seen this -- I'd seen my family dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question about times. You've indicated that you -- you left Uzdol -- left Prozor at a certain time and arrived in Uzdol at a particular time. Do you think it's possible that your times might be a little bit wrong, that in fact you might have arrived a bit later in the morning or not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't arrive later. We left early in the morning. We went on foot for part of the way and we used a vehicle for another part, but when we arrived there there was no more shooting, no more fighting. These men had withdrawn. There was some shelling in the hills. They would shell from up above occasionally. But I certainly arrived there by 10.00. I certainly arrived at my house by 10.00 at the latest, and I arrived in the village even earlier. I can't say how much time I spent in various places. I was running. I wanted to know whether my family members were still alive. You couldn't stay with others and remain there crying for an hour or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. Look, I understand and I'm not going to press you for questions about that. And my final question on that topic is: Whatever the times might be, you can say that you had begun to find the killed people well and truly by 10.00 in the morning; is that correct? And even possibly --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: By 10.00 and perhaps even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. Okay. I just want you to look at the fine one here. I anticipate your answer might be that you haven't seen it, but I just want you to look anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the fourth report. Page 6 in English, page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report without a particular time attached to it. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offer those documents for tender. It might be that they'll have to be tendered through another witness, but in any event I'm still going to offer them at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Chana?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just have a moment to look at this last document before I reply to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We may save it until a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. That's okay. I don't have to do anything else with it. Very well. Now, there are two things I've forgotten to ask and then I've finish. Would you just excuse me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Sorry. Pardon me. Yes. Very well, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Luca and Janja Zelenika, I simply neglected to ask you about them altogether and I'm sorry about that. Were there any eyewitnesses to the killing of Luca and Janja Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no one, but Ivka Stojanovic survived. But there are no eyewitnesses. They're both dead in the vicinity of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above and below the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cut you off there. Was there any person living with them at the time of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the bride Doma living with Luca, and she survived. She managed to run to the shop, the old shop and to Prozor. But the old woman was born in 1906, she was killed. But Janja lived in her house. Behind her house. Luca was Janja's aunt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What was the --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Doma is now in Djakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you just state for the record Doma's full name, please?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doma Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And did you yourself see and speak to Doma on the day of the killings?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. She ran away. She fled, and I didn't even meet her. We were in uniforms. They would hide from us. When they fled in the direction of Prozor, they even avoided us. They didn't know who was who. I didn't see her on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, how many people in the village had the name Ivka Rajic at that time?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two. There was a Mirka who had suffered a stroke, Mirka Rajic. Doma's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I didn't I think I pronounced that very clearly. It was Ivka, the name Ivka Rajic.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivka. Ivka Rajic. Both Ivkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There were two people with that name; correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two people with that name. One had the maiden name Mendes and the other's maiden number was Blazevic. The younger one who was Doma's wife. Blazevic I think her name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Were each of them killed or did one of them survive?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both killed. The elderly woman suffered a stroke and she couldn't walk. She had suffered a stroke before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much for your patience in answering my questions over a long period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Those are the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will take a break before the re-examination by the Prosecution, and then we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana. Any redirect examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. Sorry. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika, I will be asking you a few questions with your permission. I would like, first of all, to ask you about this book that the Defence showed you this morning. Could you please tell us, firstly, whose idea was it to write this book?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whose idea it was. The parish priest came to see me, told me that a memorial centre would be built and that a book would be a good idea to raise some money for the monument to be erected, funds to be raised by the -- by selling the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So it was the parish priest which approached you and not you who approached him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He approached me to give him a hand with that. He published the book, not me. I know about people from my area, about when they were born and where, and he wanted these data. I have no idea how the book eventually came to be published.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what did he say your contribution was to be to the book?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said I could give him a hand with the date of birth and places of birth in relation to those persons. He said that he would get the book printed. I'm not sure how many copies he mentioned. I'm not sure how many he sold, for that matter, but the memorial centre was eventually built. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I'll get into the details of a little later, but for now could you please go to the first page where there are all the people who were involved in this book. It's not translated on the first page. Where it says the publisher is John the Baptist Parish, Uzdol. Are you with me, Mr. Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who was the responsible person, does it say. Is this a direct translation from it?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Published by Don Milenko Dzalto, parish priest, St. John the Baptist church, year 2000. A lot had been forgotten by this time. Those dead bodies had been lying in Prozor for nine years. There was no permission to move the bodies. It was only later that the bodies were eventually moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And then it says text is yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wanted to put my name there because I had helped him, so I wouldn't take umbrage for not being included and not having my name published. He said, I put your name right there because you wrote the write-ups, and you can put the other one's name right there, too, because he proof-read the write-ups. And he put someone else's name there, too, Luksic -- Vuksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And the content editor was Gusto Vlajcic. Sorry about the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something to the effect that he entered certain corrections just in case I made errors. Improvements in terms of style in one word. He could write better than I could, and this proof-reader was probably somebody who had an even higher level of education. You need to have a higher level of education if you want to proof-read books, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Absolutely. And then there was design and print, a man called Muller from Sarajevo. Now, before I go to your part in this, could you tell us whether there was a second printing of this book or was there just one print?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was another. Some persons had been left out, so in order to include everyone, there was another edition. They had no information in relation to certain soldiers, and once this information was obtained, they published more. But I -- I didn't do any work for the next edition of this book.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, in the text, who provided the details of the cause of death, et cetera, some of the details which appears in the text? Was that yours?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of it was mine, and some of it was written by the other people. I'm not sure how they went about that. I provided most of the personal information, year of birth, that sort of thing, where people resided and what they did for a living.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That would be personal data. The personal data.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, personal data, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'll just give -- go through a couple of examples that were shown to your, I'll go to Stjepan's. I'm trying to see the number. It's at page 91. I think it's 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Stjepan, I didn't go to Stjepan, but he's on page 94-5, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Stjepan Zelic on page 95. Are you there with me?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite yet. 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: If you look at the description page, there is a description about how Stjepan died, and I go to the second paragraph towards the end, the last five lines or so. It says: "Stjepan" --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: "Stjepan ran towards the road with some soldiers chasing him and others waiting for them. So soldiers seized little Stjepan and cut his throat with a knife and mowed down his mother," et cetera. Now, when you observed Stjepan, what kind of wounds did you observe on Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the throat. I think there was a bullet hole on his head and there was something behind his ear, an abrasion possibly caused by a bullet. A cut behind one ear and a bullet hole in his head.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So that's not a correct description, is it, as it's reflected in your book -- or this book?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says he was captured, and it is not known whether he was killed by a rifle. Was this thing about a knife being used and his throat being slit, I'm not sure. I think he was killed by a rifle. He had some sort of a sweater on and his underpants. This was written seven years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you put that detail in yourself? Was that your own observation?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I did realise there were changes here to what I had originally written. I have no idea who translated my write-ups. I'm not sure if it's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Don't look at the translation, but -- that's not the true position, is it? So was that your text? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of it is and a part of it isn't. When I saw Stjepan, it was all different. He had a bullet hole in his head, and there was a cut behind one of his ears. Whether it was caused by an object or by a burst of fire, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show an autopsy, P312. This is an autopsy report of -- sorry, Your Honours. 65 ter, 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it better be explained how that autopsy report arises out of cross-examination; and secondly, how this witness can be validly shown a -- I don't mind him being shown the cause of death -- I'm sorry, the death certificates because he was the official who produced those, but an autopsy report is a pretty expert sort of thing, so I'm not sure this witness ought to be asked about autopsy reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Chana I, are you going impeach this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In fact, he's very consistent that he did not -- he did not say that his throat was sliced. It was not part of his text, and I want to show the autopsy, just mark it for identification. When the coroner comes he will no doubt produce this exhibit to show what the cause of death, which was a bullet wound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So I believe there is no need for you to show that report at all since you are not going to impeach the witness on that very point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. There is no intention whatsoever to impeach this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. I'll move along.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you page for Ruza Zelic. Page 60. Page 60, Your Honour. Thank you, counsel. Now, counsel for the Defence showed you this particular text of Ruza Zelic.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And it talks about hand grenades. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is this your text? Is this what you wrote yourself?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent. Some details concerning the military matters have been changed. I'm not sure who changed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So there were others who contributed to the text. Would that be an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were others who added things later on. It was not written all at once. I wrote my contribution within a space of two or three days by hand. They took it away. There were soldiers there in this book that I didn't know. They wanted their photographs. And some descriptions were made of people who were not from my area. Therefore, I have no idea who added the other details later on. As for their personal information, this is something that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So when you said you didn't know anything about hand grenades being thrown by this particular witness, you were being truthful to this Court, were you not?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely truthful. There was no way I could see it. The woman had got away quite far from where I was. There was no way I could have seen if she had thrown a hand grenade or not, and her body was found dead 500 metres further down the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Right. Now, I'd like to ask you about this matter of assistance which were given to some people in the village. What was the criteria for assistance to be given?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was so that the soldiers could have enough food, but there was civilians and children in the village who didn't have enough food. We were given bread, canned meat, cold cuts, that sort of thing. When we came to Prozor they would lend us a TAM truck once in two or three months to transport the supplies back to our village. Beans, flour, whatever they happened to have in stock. They wouldn't give it to us very often, but every now and then they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I think I didn't put my question to your clearly enough to you. I mean after the war, financial assistance given.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, I don't know. Those who lived alone with no income received social assistance. Every three months they would receive 40 German marks, those without an income. It was a social fund for those who don't have a job, for the elderly, disabled people, that sort of thing. I'm not sure if it still works like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: What about military people, those who were in the HVO and served in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who served in the HVO are now gone. Those who have a job are fine. Those who don't, don't. Those who are retired and receiving a pension, maybe some others, got certificates from their doctors. Those whose parents had been killed may still be receiving compensation, but the civilians victims have no privileges and no compensation coming their way.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And for the military, did they have to have certificates before they were given financial aid?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They needed some proof as to how long they had served in the army, and then wherever they were wounded, the relevant local command would issue a certificate. If they were killed, one of their parents was supposed to bring a death certificate. The committee requested about ten or 15 different documents to be brought. If they had their parents still alive, they would receive less money than if the wife and children were still alive. That was after the war, and I have no idea who provides all this assistance. Maybe it's one of the veterans associations.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: It was essential to have a certificate, and you were shown the MFI 316 by the Defence. If you could look at it again, please. This is in respect of Mr. Domin Rajic. It has come up on your screen again, Mr. Zelenika. Now, when you were shown this document, you said there was something you wanted to explain. What was that?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everyone should have it then. Why didn't he have it? He couldn't have received assistance if he had died on the 14th of September. But his son Stipo who lives in Zagreb, and he's studying to become a dentist, maybe he needed something. I don't know. Why would he be receiving assistance if he was killed on the 14th of September, 1993? He has only one son who is in Zagreb, and he studying to become a dentist or perhaps has already completed his studies. I am not sure why he was given anything at all. Or Kata Ljubic for that matter. She has a son in Zagreb studying theology. She never asked for anything, for her household or anything like that. I have no idea, the municipality, whether they gave any form of assistance. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Do you say that they should not have got it? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was issued in 1993, the 27th of November. Assistance to a dead man. How can someone who is dead possibly receive assistance? This was issued later on, the 27th of November, and they were killed on the 14th of September. Must be something about their children over in Zagreb, the municipality helping them with their expenses, travel expenses, that sort of thing. Someone in the brigade would probably know about these things. It was probably some sort of discount or -- or reduced fees for accommodation over in Zagreb because their parents were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Zelenika. Now, I want to ask you to look at MFI 317. And this is in respect of Kata Ljubic. This is another certificate that were shown.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. It's not the same, is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, it's another one.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on the 9th of May, 1996. So there you have it. She died in 1993, and this is much later on. If this is by way of assistance, then it can't be for her. It's probably one of her children who was supposed to be the beneficiary. It can't be her. It must be someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's fine. First of all, can you look at the first? It says HVO unit that she belonged to was the 42nd Home Guard Battalion of the Rama Brigade. Was the home guard part of the Rama Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all called the 42nd Home Guard. This was no professional unit. The professional unit was the 4th Split Unit, those units over in Croatia, and we were the so-called home guard, all of us. I'm not sure what the exact term was. The professional units were over in the Republic of Croatia. We weren't out to conquer anything. We just wanted to hold onto our lines of defence, and regrettably we failed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. And when it talks about the circumstances of her death, it says: It was during the attack of MOS forces against Uzdol while, and it says there, carrying out the order on the defence front line. Now, to your knowledge is this an accurate position? Did she die on the front line?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the line. It's not the front line. She died on the way from her house to Domin's house. She was running from those people pursuing her. I'm not sure who wrote this. Someone was probably looking for something.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Now, you also said when you were being cross examined by the Defence that some people received assistance and others did not receive what they should be.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Domin, Kata, Mara should have got it and all the others. But there's no one to request that they be given compensation or assistance. I don't know. Why should she be requesting compensation if all she ever did was bake several dozens of loaves of bread? What should soldiers be given then?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But it was important to claim that you were a member of the HVO before you claimed assistance, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I have an objection to raise there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I don't know if it's being advanced now that these claims are somehow false claims. What we have is the letters that have been tendered without objection indicating that these people were members of the HVO. Now, this witness can be asked whether he knew whether they were members of the HVO or not. That's fine. That arises out of cross-examination. But it's not legitimate to ask the questions that are now being asked, you know, in a leading form --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So I object, Your Honour. And if you look at the -- at the -- I think -- anyway, my objection might have been overwhelmed by events here, by what the witness said, but I do object to that line of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe the witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but could I -- could I ask the witness whether he thought they were a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika, was Kata a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was a member, yes. I did tell you right at the outset she was there. She was helping us. I'm not sure what her official position was. I don't know. But not for as long as it claims here in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were families ever provided such documents as a favour for entitlements?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never seen these certificates before.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Give me a moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Lastly, Mr. Zelenika, you were not an eyewitness to any of the events in Uzdol on that morning, on the 14th of September, having arrived there at 10.00 in the morning after everything had -- everything was over. Is that a correct position?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything was over. They were all dead. I saw them personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions from Judges? Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to discuss a few details firstly. On the 14th in the morning, on the 14th of September, when you set off in the direction of Uzdol from Prozor, at what time did you say that you set off?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you when exactly. When we heard in Prozor that Uzdol was burning, we then got up, checked to see whether there was enough fuel in the TAM vehicle and set off in the direction of Prozor. I don't know when it was exactly, but we drove for about seven or eight kilometres in the TAM vehicle and then we carried on on foot. We took a short route to continue there on foot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. How long did that take you approximately?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a dirt road. You drive for about half an hour, perhaps a little more, and then there's a hill. You can't proceed rapidly. You don't know whether the army troops or the HVO are there. There's a plateau up there, whereas we're down below. When we reached that point, everyone was dead. Perhaps we got there by 8.00 or 8.30 at the latest. Perhaps we reached the first people there near the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 8.00 or 8.30. What was the weather like? Was it raining?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't raining. At the time it was dry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You went to the building that we've been calling the school directly?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First I saw Pero Kovcalija. Then I saw a soldier, a MOS soldier, an army soldier, and then Slavko Mendes and then I headed towards my house. I didn't head towards the school. The school is the last building I went to. When I returned from Kriz and Rajici, it was only at that point that I went to the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you arrived in Uzdol you met a child on the road who told you --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who said that they had killed his mother?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I met Ivan Stojanovic near the village called Perici, halfway between Uzdol and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he told you the name of the person who had killed his mother?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, My mother is dead. They have killed my mother. He said, Sabo from Here has killed my mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Saban?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later he died. He was a construction worker and he fell off a building and died. He didn't die in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how is it that the child knew him?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was near Here, the village of Here. Here and Kriz are not very far. Perhaps two, two and a half kilometres away. And then he went down to that shop. You would go there on foot. You wouldn't take the road to go around. And he would go to Uzdol. All the children went to school together in Uzdol, Croatian children and Bosniak children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the child told you that the person who had allegedly killed his mother was in uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. It was a soldier. He was wearing a military uniform on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you went to the school you met the cameraman there.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was someone there, but the troops had already assembled there. There was the cameraman. So it was hard to distinguish everyone. You'd look at the dead bodies and the other people. A mass of troops and civilians were assembled there. I can't remember things exactly. There was someone with a camera, but I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the person who accompanied you later to shoot the scene of the incidents.

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which organisation was he a member of or which institution? Was he a member of --

utterances.speaker: KAZO ZELENIKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
